items.title: David N. Baker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Lynne Arriale, who’s been wanting to study with me for some time

ctx.x: different ways to call the muse. I write so much music that usually I don’t have a chance to sit around and wait for inspiration. I have to write because I’m being paid to write. So I’ve devised a number of schemes. Some of them come from other teachers. I’ve had a teacher tell me – when I wrote the piece Kosbro, he said, “Why don’t you go sit in the auditorium where the piece will probably be played and imagine what you’re going to hear.” And I did. And I sat down and I wrote the piece. I have no notion of where…

So when I write a piece now – and this is what I tell people who want to study with me, and I’m going to say this to [pianist-composer] Lynne Arriale, who’s been wanting to study with me for some time – what I do now is I lay the theme out. I turn it on its side and see what it looks like if I put all the notes in one chord. I see what it looks like if I take the last two notes and put them in the front, to see if it, in fact, can bear fruit. So what you end up doing is trying to use all that material. You look…
